narrative:
The model predicts you have a 19% chance of failing your final year, which is high enough that the school requires you to take remedial courses as a precaution.

The three factors that most strongly shaped this prediction were your lack of desire to pursue higher education, your reason for choosing this school, and the fact that you have had no previous class failures. Surprisingly, not wanting higher education was the single biggest influence pushing the model toward predicting failure. Because every student who passed expressed a clear ambition to continue studying after school, your answer of “no” stood out as a strong warning sign to the model.

Your reason for selecting the school (its reputation) worked in the opposite direction and pulled the prediction back toward passing. Most students who passed chose the school for its academic reputation, so this choice helped your chances. Having zero past failures also nudged the outcome slightly toward passing, since students who succeed usually have similarly clean records.

Even though these last two factors helped, they were not enough to overcome the strong negative signal from your plans after school. To improve, you should seriously reflect on your longer-term goals. Speaking with a counselor about why higher education feels unimportant to you right now could help you either rediscover motivation or find a different path that still keeps your final-year grades on track. Taking the remedial courses seriously is a good first step.
